title: Aristotle's Metaphysics
orientation: This chapter opens Russell's extended treatment of Aristotle by sketching his life and character and then working through his core metaphysical apparatus: his criticism of Plato's theory of Ideas, his own doctrine of universals, the distinction between matter and form, the concepts of potentiality and actuality, his theology of an unmoved mover, and his doctrine of the soul. Understanding this apparatus matters because, via medieval Scholasticism, it dominated Western philosophy and science for roughly two thousand years, and much of modern philosophy's vocabulary (substance, essence, potentiality, category) descends directly from it.
historical_background: Aristotle was born about 384 B.C. at Stagyra in Thrace, son of the court physician to the Macedonian king; he studied under Plato at the Academy for nearly twenty years until Plato's death in 348-7 B.C., later tutored the young Alexander (from 343 B.C.), and returned to Athens from 335 to 323 B.C. to found his own school and write most of his surviving works. After Alexander's death he was indicted for impiety and fled Athens, dying in 322 B.C. Russell stresses that Aristotle came at the very end of the creative period of Greek philosophy, so that his posthumous authority -- almost as unquestioned in the late Middle Ages as that of the Church -- became, in science and philosophy alike, a serious obstacle that had to be overturned by the intellectual revolutions beginning in the seventeenth century.
philosophical_problems: Does Plato's theory of Ideas survive Aristotle's criticisms, and can Aristotle's alternative account of universals do better?
What is the relationship between 'matter' and 'form,' and does this distinction do genuine metaphysical work?
Can the concept of 'potentiality' be used as a fundamental, irreducible notion without concealing confusion?
What kind of cause could an eternal, unmoved 'first cause' of motion be?
Is the human soul, or any part of it, immortal, and in what sense?

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Central subject: Russell examines his biography, his critique of Plato's Ideas, his doctrines of universals, matter and form, potentiality and actuality, his theology of the unmoved mover, and his account of the soul and mind.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Constant point of comparison; Russell describes Aristotle's metaphysics as 'Plato diluted by common sense,' and traces how far Aristotle's doctrines of universals and form remain covertly Platonic despite his explicit criticisms of the theory of Ideas.

philosophers_discussed.name: Alexander the Great
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Discussed as Aristotle's pupil (from age thirteen); Russell argues, against common assumption, that Aristotle's influence on Alexander was probably negligible, and that Aristotle's political theorizing was oblivious to the world-transforming empire Alexander was building.

philosophers_discussed.name: Zeller
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted at length for his judgement that Aristotle 'had only half emancipated himself... from Plato's tendency to hypostatise ideas,' supporting Russell's own view that Aristotle's forms remain covertly Platonic.

schools_discussed: Platonism (as the doctrine Aristotle criticizes and partly retains)
Medieval Scholasticism (as heir to Aristotle's doctrines of universals, essence, and matter/form)

core_concepts.name: The Third Man argument against Plato's theory of Ideas
core_concepts.plain_explanation: If a particular man is a man because he resembles the ideal Man, then that resemblance itself needs explaining -- which requires a still more ideal 'third man' that both the particular man and the ideal Man resemble, and so on without end.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's argument, already foreshadowed in Plato's own Parmenides, that when several individuals share a predicate, this sharing cannot be explained by their all resembling a further individual of the same kind (however 'ideal'), since that would require a yet more ideal exemplar to explain the new resemblance, generating an infinite regress.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It shows decisively, in Russell's judgement, that shared predicates cannot be explained by resemblance to a super-particular 'Idea' of the same logical type as ordinary things.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Already present in Plato's own self-criticism in the Parmenides; developed as a formal argument by Aristotle against the theory of Ideas.
examples: Socrates is both a man and an animal, raising the question whether the Ideal Man is also an Ideal Animal, and if so, whether there must be as many ideal animals as species
competing_positions: Plato's theory of Ideas, which the argument is directed against
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Left the problem of universals unresolved rather than solved, since Aristotle's own alternative doctrine was, in Russell's view, far from clear -- 'it was this lack of clarity that made possible the medieval controversy between nominalists and realists.'

core_concepts.name: Universals and substances ('this' versus 'such')
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A proper name like 'Napoleon' picks out one particular, unrepeatable thing; a word like 'man' or 'white' can apply to many different things. Aristotle calls what a proper name signifies a 'substance,' and what a general word signifies a 'universal.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's definition: 'By the term universal I mean that which is of such a nature as to be predicated of many subjects, by individual that which is not thus predicated.' A substance is a 'this'; a universal is a 'such,' indicating a sort of thing rather than a particular thing, and (Aristotle holds) cannot itself be a substance, since substance is 'peculiar' to one thing while a universal is common to many.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is Aristotle's proposed replacement for Plato's Ideas: what is common to many red things ('redness') depends for its being on there being red things, but not vice versa -- yet, as Russell shows, this common-sense-seeming asymmetry does not survive careful analysis.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out in Aristotle's On Interpretation and Categories.
examples: Football (a universal-like activity) could not exist without football-players, though it could exist without this or that particular player
Redness cannot exist without some subject, but can exist without this or that particular subject
objections: Russell argues the supposed asymmetry is illusory: just as a quality cannot exist without some subject, a subject cannot exist without some quality either -- so the 'true ground of the distinction is, in fact, linguistic; it is derived from syntax,' not metaphysics
competing_positions: Plato's theory that universals (Ideas) are themselves substantial, independently existing things
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly generated the medieval dispute between nominalists (who deny universals any extra-linguistic reality) and realists (who affirm it), since Aristotle's own position was left unclear.

core_concepts.name: Matter and Form
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Take a bronze sphere: the bronze is its 'matter,' the sphericity is its 'form.' More generally, whatever a thing is made of is its matter, and the shape or organizing structure that makes that stuff into 'a thing' at all is its form.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's doctrine that concrete substances are compounds of matter (potentiality) and form (the principle that confers definiteness, unity, and actuality); form is said to be more real and more substantial than matter, and things become more 'actual' as they acquire more form.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It let Aristotle explain unity and individuation (why a lump of marble becomes 'a statue,' a 'thing') and, extended teleologically, why living organisms and even the cosmos develop toward ever-greater actuality and likeness to God.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Aristotle, in explicit reworking of Platonic metaphysics, chiefly in the Metaphysics.
examples: A bronze sphere: bronze is matter, sphericity is form
A calm sea: water is matter, smoothness is form
The soul as 'the form of the body,' giving it organic unity of purpose
objections: Zeller's criticism (quoted by Russell) that Aristotle 'had only half emancipated himself... from Plato's tendency to hypostatise ideas,' since forms, like Ideas, are treated as substantial and more real than matter

Russell's own objection: if two brass spheres are made, does each have its own particular sphericity (making form unknowable, contrary to Aristotle's system) or the same universal sphericity (making form indistinguishable from a Platonic Idea)? Aristotle has no clear escape from this dilemma
competing_positions: Plato's theory that Forms/Ideas exist independently of any matter that exemplifies them
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became central to medieval Scholastic metaphysics and to Aristotle's own doctrine of the soul as 'the form of the body.'

core_concepts.name: The Unmoved Mover and Aristotle's theology
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Since anything that moves must be caused to move by something else, and that chain cannot regress forever, there must be an ultimate source of motion that is itself unmoved -- and Aristotle argues this Unmoved Mover causes motion not by pushing things (like one billiard ball hitting another) but by being loved and desired, the way a beautiful object of thought moves us without itself moving.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's argument for God as an eternal, unmoved, immaterial substance -- 'pure form and pure actuality' -- that causes motion as a final cause (the object of desire and of thought) rather than as an efficient cause; God's activity is pure self-directed thought, 'a thinking on thinking,' with no knowledge of or love for the world.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It supplies Aristotle's answer to the question of what starts the whole causal order of change moving, and it frames the universe as continually 'evolving' toward greater form and likeness to God -- an optimistic, teleological picture of nature.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out at the end of Aristotle's Physics and in Metaphysics Book Lambda (Theta), which Aristotle himself called 'theology.'
examples: The claim that there are 'either forty-seven or fifty-five' unmoved movers tied to the motions of the heavenly spheres, whose relation to a single God is left unclear
Aristotle's four kinds of cause -- material, formal, efficient, and final -- illustrated by a sculptor making a statue
objections: Russell notes God, on this view, cannot love or care for the world (since attending to anything less than perfect would derogate from divine perfection), so -- unlike the Christian God -- 'it is impossible that God should love men,' though men must love God
To a modern mind, Russell notes, a cause of change is naturally thought to be a previous change, making the very idea of an eternally unmoved first cause of motion difficult to accept
competing_positions: The Christian conception of a providential God who loves and knows His creation, which later theologians had to reconcile uneasily with the inherited Aristotelian God
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became, through Scholasticism, one of the chief classical arguments for God's existence (the 'unmoved mover' or 'first cause' argument) adopted and adapted by medieval Christian philosophers such as Aquinas.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological: Aristotle's own term for this branch of his philosophy was 'theology.'

core_concepts.name: Potentiality and Actuality
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A block of marble is only a 'potential' statue -- it could become one, but is not yet one; once it has been given the sculptor's form, it has become 'actual.' Aristotle uses this potential/actual distinction to describe all change as a movement from less to more form.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Bare matter is conceived as pure potentiality of form; change is the process by which potentiality is realized as actuality; that which has more form is more 'actual,' and God, having no matter, is pure actuality with no potentiality and therefore no possibility of change.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It underlies Aristotle's optimistic, teleological view that the universe develops toward ever more organized, actualized (and hence more divine) states.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Aristotle as the dynamic complement to the matter-form distinction.
examples: 'A block of marble is a potential statue,' meaning 'from a block of marble, by suitable acts, a statue is produced'
objections: Russell argues potentiality is a convenient shorthand only if it can be translated away into statements where it does not appear; used as a fundamental, irreducible concept, it 'always conceals confusion of thought,' and Aristotle's use of it is 'one of the bad points in his system'

core_concepts.name: The soul as form of the body, and the immortality of mind alone
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The soul is not a separate ghostly substance inside the body; it is what makes a body one organized, purposeful living thing -- the way a shape makes a lump of wax into a particular seal-impression. But within the soul, Aristotle distinguishes a higher part, 'mind,' which alone might survive the body's death.
core_concepts.precise_definition: In Aristotle's On the Soul, the soul is 'the actuality of a body' having life potentially within it -- related to the body as form to matter -- and is therefore, for the most part, inseparable from the body and perishes with it. Mind (nous), however, is described as 'an independent substance implanted within the soul,' timeless because its objects (mathematics, philosophy) are timeless, and 'incapable of being destroyed'; the Nicomachean Ethics adds that the rational soul's contemplative activity is the highest happiness, in which a person 'shares in the divine life' impersonally rather than as an individual.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It produced centuries of controversy (Averroes and his followers held Aristotle taught no personal immortality at all) and set the template for later distinctions between an animating 'soul' and a separately immortal 'intellect' or 'reason.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed across Aristotle's On the Soul and Nicomachean Ethics.
examples: The eye cannot see when parted from the body, illustrating that an organ's purpose (and hence the soul's work) depends on the living organic whole
Self-nutrition as the only psychic power possessed by plants, versus sensation and motivity in animals, versus thought in the part of humans called 'mind'
competing_positions: The Pythagorean doctrine of transmigration of souls, which Aristotle explicitly ridicules
Averroes's interpretation that Aristotle taught no immortality at all -- a reading Dante associated with the 'Epicureans' he places in hell
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Because mind, for Aristotle, is impersonal and shared rather than individual, Russell concludes that on the most natural reading its 'immortality' is not personal survival but a shared participation in the divine -- 'if he succeeded completely, he would have ceased to exist as a separate person.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Closely tied to Aristotle's theology, since mind's timeless objects link it to the divine, unmoved mover.

arguments.title: The Third Man argument against the theory of Ideas
premises: A particular man is said to be a man because he resembles the Idea of Man.
If resemblance to an ideal exemplar explains why particulars share a predicate, the ideal exemplar must itself be of the same general kind as the particulars, sharing the predicate too.
But then the ideal exemplar's resemblance to the particulars (and to itself as exemplary) requires a further, still more ideal exemplar to explain it, and so on without end.
arguments.conclusion: When a number of individuals share a predicate, this cannot be explained by their relation to something of the same kind as themselves, however ideal -- Plato's theory of Ideas, as usually stated, cannot be right.
arguments.explanation: Aristotle exploits the fact that Plato's Ideas are themselves treated as a kind of super-particular (an Ideal Man who is, in a sense, also a man), which triggers an infinite regress rather than terminating an explanation.
implications: This left the problem of universals open rather than solved, since Aristotle's alternative doctrine of universals was, in Russell's judgement, unclear -- fueling the later medieval nominalist-realist controversy

arguments.title: The common-sense argument for the asymmetric dependence of universals on particulars
premises: Football could not exist without football-players, though football could exist without this or that particular player.
Similarly, sweetness could not exist without sweet things, and redness could not exist without red things.
But football-players could exist even if they never played football, and a face that is usually red could turn pale without ceasing to be a face.
arguments.conclusion: What is meant by an adjective (a universal) is dependent for its being on what is meant by a proper name (a substance), but not vice versa.
arguments.explanation: This is Aristotle's common-sense-seeming basis for holding that substances are metaphysically prior to universals -- substances can exist without any particular quality, while qualities cannot exist without some subject.
objections: Russell argues the asymmetry is illusory: though football-players need not play this or that game of football, they cannot exist without doing something; a subject cannot exist without some quality, even though it can exist without this or that particular quality. The 'true ground of the distinction is, in fact, linguistic; it is derived from syntax' -- proper names, adjectives, and relation-words -- not from any real metaphysical difference
implications: Metaphysicians who read syntactic distinctions (subject/predicate) directly onto reality (substance/universal) may be projecting features of language onto the world without justification

arguments.title: The argument for an Unmoved Mover as the source of all motion
premises: Whatever moves is moved by something else.
This chain of movers cannot regress infinitely; there must be a first mover.
The first mover must itself be unmoved, eternal, substance, and pure actuality, since anything moved is only partly actual.
A cause of motion can operate either by itself being in motion (an efficient cause, like a billiard ball) or by being an object of desire or thought (a final cause) without itself moving.
arguments.conclusion: There exists an eternal, unmoved, immaterial God who causes all motion in the universe as a final cause -- by being loved and desired -- rather than as an ordinary efficient cause.
arguments.explanation: This is Aristotle's central theological argument, developed at the end of the Physics and in the Metaphysics; it identifies God with pure thought thinking itself, whose perfection draws the imperfect, changing world toward it.
objections: Aristotle's own text creates an unresolved tension by later speaking of forty-seven or fifty-five unmoved movers, without clarifying their relation to the single God described elsewhere
Russell notes that, to a modern mind, a cause of change is naturally another change, so an eternally unmoved first cause of motion is a difficult notion to make sense of
implications: Became, via Scholasticism, one of the classical philosophical arguments for God's existence
Implies a God who cannot love or know the imperfect world, since attending to anything less than perfect would compromise divine self-sufficiency

arguments.title: Zeller's criticism that Aristotle's forms remain covertly Platonic
premises: Aristotle intends 'form' to be something quite different from a Platonic 'Idea,' dependent on matter for its embodiment.
Yet Aristotle also holds that forms are substances, more real than matter, and that a form is identical with a thing's essence.
The further a form is removed from ordinary sense-experience, the more it is treated as an object of pure intellectual intuition, exactly as Plato's Ideas were.
arguments.conclusion: Aristotle 'had only half emancipated himself... from Plato's tendency to hypostatise ideas' -- his change to Plato's metaphysics is, in substance, less radical than he represents it as being.
arguments.explanation: Russell endorses this criticism and extends it with his own dilemma: if two brass spheres are made, either each has its own particular sphericity (which would make form unknowable, contradicting Aristotle's claim that more form means more knowability) or they share one universal sphericity (which collapses form back into something very like a Platonic Idea).
implications: Suggests that the classical dispute between 'Platonism' and 'Aristotelianism' regarding universals is less sharp than the ancient rivalry between the two philosophers might suggest

key_distinctions: The four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final
Efficient causation (moving by being itself in motion) vs. final causation (moving by being loved or desired)
Soul (bound to and perishing with the body) vs. mind/nous (timeless, possibly indestructible)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell frames the entire chapter as a running comparison with Plato: Aristotle's theory of universals is his answer to Plato's theory of Ideas, and his doctrine of matter and form is presented as 'Plato diluted by common sense' -- a partial retreat from, rather than a clean break with, Platonism.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Aristotle's unclear doctrine of universals generated the medieval controversy between nominalists and realists; his unmoved-mover theology became a template for later natural theology (echoed, Russell notes, all the way to Spinoza's view that men must love God though God cannot love men); and his soul/mind distinction shaped later medieval and Scholastic debates over personal immortality.
political_social_context: Russell situates Aristotle's biography against Macedonian court politics -- his father's position as royal physician, his tutorship of the young Alexander, and his eventual indictment for impiety and flight from Athens after Alexander's death, when the Athenians turned on Macedonian sympathizers.
religion_science_culture_context: Aristotle's theology, in which God is pure self-contemplating thought indifferent to the world, sits uneasily beside the later Christian conception of a providential, loving God -- a tension Russell notes explicitly when comparing Aristotle to Spinoza on this point.
russell_presentation: Russell opens by insisting Aristotle be judged fairly on both sides: his merits relative to his predecessors were enormous, but his two-thousand-year unquestioned authority did enormous damage to later science and philosophy, for which his successors, not Aristotle himself, are chiefly to blame. He characterizes Aristotle's temperament as unemotional, professorial, and pedestrian compared to Plato's 'Bacchic enthusiasm,' and is skeptical that Aristotle had much real influence on Alexander despite their famous tutorial relationship. Turning to metaphysics, Russell credits Aristotle's criticism of Plato's Ideas (especially the Third Man argument) as genuinely decisive, but judges Aristotle's own replacement doctrine of universals to be unclear, and -- following Zeller -- argues that Aristotle's doctrine of form remains covertly Platonic, exposing Aristotle to versions of his own objections against Plato. He presents the theology of the unmoved mover in detail, including the puzzling multiplication of movers, and treats Aristotle's optimistic, teleological picture of a universe evolving toward God as intellectually interesting but resting on the dubious, unanalysed notion of potentiality. On the soul, Russell reconstructs Aristotle's view carefully, concluding that the most natural interpretation makes the immortality of 'mind' impersonal rather than a survival of the individual self.
critical_context: Common scholarly caveat: Russell's claim that Aristotle's forms are simply Platonic Ideas by another name (endorsing Zeller's older interpretive line) is not universally accepted; many twentieth- and twenty-first-century Aristotle scholars argue that Aristotle's forms, unlike Plato's Ideas, are genuinely immanent in and inseparable from the particulars they inform (except in the special case of God), making Russell's dilemma about 'particular versus universal sphericity' less damaging than he suggests once Aristotle's own technical apparatus (e.g. the individual/universal distinction within form itself) is taken into account.
key_takeaways: Russell judges Aristotle's Third Man argument to be a genuinely decisive objection to Plato's theory of Ideas, even though it left the problem of universals unsolved.

Aristotle's own doctrine of universals ('substance' as 'this,' 'universal' as 'such') rests, on Russell's analysis, on a merely linguistic (subject/predicate) distinction rather than a genuine metaphysical one.

The matter-form distinction (illustrated by a bronze sphere) lets Aristotle explain unity and individuation, but Russell -- following Zeller -- argues Aristotle's 'forms' remain covertly Platonic, since they are treated as substantial and more real than matter.

Aristotle's theology argues for an eternal, unmoved, self-contemplating God who moves the universe as a final cause (by being loved), not an efficient cause -- yet the text also mentions forty-seven or fifty-five unmoved movers without resolving their relation to God.
Russell criticizes Aristotle's concept of 'potentiality,' used as a fundamental notion, as one of the genuinely 'bad points' in his system.

Aristotle's doctrine of the soul makes the soul (bound to the body) perishable but 'mind' potentially indestructible and impersonal, so that, on the most natural reading, its immortality is not the survival of an individual person.
study_notes:
This chapter rewards close attention to Russell's recurring method: state Aristotle's doctrine in its plainest, most common-sense form; then show the 'Platonic modification' hiding inside it; then test whether the doctrine can be made precise without collapsing into either bare common sense or unreconstructed Platonism. Applied to universals, this method shows that what looks like a metaphysical claim (substances are prior to universals) is really a disguised grammatical observation about proper names versus adjectives. Applied to matter and form, it shows that 'form' quietly does the same philosophical work that Plato's 'Ideas' did, despite Aristotle's explicit criticism of Plato.

It is worth tracking the theology section carefully as a case study in how ancient metaphysical argument gets inherited by later religious philosophy: the unmoved-mover argument becomes, centuries later, one of Aquinas's Five Ways, even though Aristotle's own God -- who cannot love or know the world -- is theologically very unlike the Christian God who eventually inherits the argument.

Finally, the soul/mind distinction is a good test case for reading philosophical texts charitably but critically: Aristotle's language about mind being 'indestructible' can sound like a doctrine of personal immortality, but Russell shows that, read in context (mind as impersonal, timeless, shared by all who think correctly about the same objects), the doctrine amounts to something closer to Spinoza's idea of participating in an eternal, impersonal aspect of reality than to surviving as 'you.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: What a proper name like 'Socrates' picks out: a particular, individual thing, as opposed to a general quality it might have.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Aristotle's primary sense, an individual thing that is neither predicable of, nor present in, a subject; a 'this' rather than a 'such,' contrasted with universals, which are common to many things.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A general word or quality, like 'man' or 'white,' that can apply to many different particular things.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: That which is 'of such a nature as to be predicated of many subjects'; Aristotle denies universals are themselves substances, since substance must be peculiar to one thing.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Matter is what a thing is made of; form is the shape or structure that makes that material into a definite, particular thing.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's hylomorphic distinction: matter is potentiality, form is the actualizing principle that confers definiteness and, in Aristotle's view, greater reality and substantiality on a compound.
related_concepts: Soul as form of the body

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A block of marble is only a 'potential' statue; once shaped, it becomes an 'actual' one. Change, for Aristotle, is the movement from potential to actual.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's dynamic complement to matter and form: matter is pure potentiality of form, actuality is the realized state; that which has more form is more actual, with God as pure actuality and no potentiality whatsoever.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's God: an eternal being that causes all motion in the universe without itself ever moving, by being the object of love and desire rather than by pushing things.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's First Cause: an eternal, immaterial substance, pure form and pure actuality, that causes motion as a final cause; identified with self-contemplating divine thought, 'a thinking on thinking.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The properties something cannot lose without ceasing to be itself.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's term for what a thing is 'by its very nature' -- those properties definitional of it and of its species; Russell calls the notion 'muddle-headed' and 'incapable of precision.'

questions.prompt: What is the 'Third Man' argument, and what does it show against Plato's theory of Ideas?
questions.answer: If a man is a man because he resembles the ideal Man, there must be a still more ideal man to which both ordinary men and the ideal man are similar, generating an infinite regress. It shows that when several individuals share a predicate, this cannot be explained by their relation to a further individual of the same kind, however ideal.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as one of the strongest arguments Aristotle brings against Plato, largely inherited from Plato's own self-criticism in the Parmenides.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what is the real, underlying basis for Aristotle's distinction between substances and universals?
questions.answer: Not a genuine metaphysical difference, but a linguistic one derived from syntax: proper names, adjectives, and relation-words function differently in sentences, and Aristotle (like metaphysicians after him) has interpreted these syntactical differences metaphysically.
questions.explanation: Russell's critique reduces Aristotle's substance/universal distinction to a projection of grammar onto reality.

questions.prompt: Compare Aristotle's doctrine of form with Plato's theory of Ideas, using Zeller's criticism quoted in the chapter.
questions.answer: Aristotle intends form to differ from a Platonic Idea by being embodied in matter rather than existing independently. But Zeller argues Aristotle 'had only half emancipated himself' from Plato: forms are still treated as substances, more real than matter and identical with a thing's essence, and the further removed from sense-experience, the more they are treated as objects of pure intellectual intuition -- just like Plato's Ideas.
questions.explanation: Russell endorses this criticism and adds his own dilemma about whether two identical objects share one form or each has its own particular form.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Aristotle's argument for an Unmoved Mover.
questions.answer: Premise 1: Whatever moves is moved by something else. Premise 2: This chain cannot regress infinitely, so there must be a first mover. Premise 3: The first mover must itself be unmoved, eternal substance, and pure actuality. Premise 4: A cause can move things either by itself moving (efficient cause) or by being loved/desired (final cause), without itself moving. Conclusion: There exists an eternal, unmoved, immaterial God, pure thought thinking itself, that causes all motion as a final cause.
questions.explanation: This argument became, through Scholasticism, a template for later 'first cause' arguments for God's existence.

questions.prompt: How does Aristotle's God differ from the Christian conception of a providential deity, according to Russell?
questions.answer: Aristotle's God cannot know of or love the imperfect, changing world, since attending to anything less than perfect would derogate from its own perfection; its thinking is only 'a thinking on thinking.' Men must love God, but it is impossible that God should love men -- a position Russell compares to Spinoza's.
questions.explanation: This highlights a major theological difference between Aristotle's unmoved mover and the personal, providential God of later Christian theology that nonetheless borrowed his 'first cause' argument.

questions.prompt: What distinction does Aristotle draw between 'soul' and 'mind,' and what does this imply about immortality?
questions.answer: The soul is 'the actuality of a body' having life potentially in it, bound to and perishing with the body except perhaps in part; 'mind,' however, is described as an independent, timeless substance implanted within the soul, incapable of destruction, because its objects (mathematics, philosophy) are themselves timeless. Since mind is impersonal and shared rather than individual, its immortality is most naturally read not as the survival of a particular person but as a shared participation in the divine.
questions.explanation: Russell concludes that if a man succeeded completely in increasing the divine element in his nature, 'he would have ceased to exist as a separate person.'

flashcards.back: The bronze is the matter; the sphericity (shape) is the form.

flashcards.front: What does Zeller argue about Aristotle's doctrine of form?
flashcards.back: That Aristotle 'had only half emancipated himself... from Plato's tendency to hypostatise ideas' -- forms remain covertly Platonic.

flashcards.front: What does 'potentiality' mean when applied to a block of marble?
flashcards.back: That 'from a block of marble, by suitable acts, a statue is produced' -- it is a potential statue.

flashcards.front: Why does Russell criticize Aristotle's use of 'potentiality'?
flashcards.back: Because used as a fundamental, irreducible concept (rather than one always translatable away), it 'always conceals confusion of thought.'

flashcards.front: What are Aristotle's four kinds of cause?
How does Aristotle's Unmoved Mover cause motion?
flashcards.back: As a final cause -- by being loved and desired -- not as an efficient cause that is itself in motion.

flashcards.front: How many unmoved movers does Aristotle's astronomy imply, and is their relation to God clarified?
flashcards.back: Forty-seven or fifty-five, according to astronomical considerations; their relation to a single God is not made clear.

flashcards.front: Can Aristotle's God love or know the world, according to Russell?
flashcards.back: No -- attending to anything less than perfect would derogate from divine perfection; God's thought is 'a thinking on thinking' about itself alone.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between 'soul' and 'mind' in Aristotle's psychology?
flashcards.back: Soul is the form of the body, bound up with and perishing with it; mind is a higher, more independent, timeless part, possibly indestructible, because its objects (mathematics, philosophy) are timeless.

quiz.prompt: Who tutored Alexander the Great starting in 343 B.C.?
quiz.explanation: Aristotle became Alexander's tutor at age thirteen; Russell doubts the tutorship had much real influence on Alexander.
quiz.related_concept: The Unmoved Mover and Aristotle's theology

quiz.prompt: What does Aristotle's 'Third Man' argument target?
options: The doctrine of the golden mean
The doctrine of the unmoved mover
quiz.explanation: It argues that explaining shared predicates by resemblance to an ideal exemplar of the same kind produces an infinite regress.
quiz.related_concept: The Third Man argument against Plato's theory of Ideas

quiz.prompt: In the example of a bronze sphere, what does Aristotle call the sphericity?
quiz.explanation: Bronze is the matter; sphericity, the shape conferred, is the form.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, Aristotle's doctrine of form is entirely free of the Platonic tendency to treat abstract entities as independently existing substances.
quiz.explanation: Russell, citing Zeller, argues Aristotle's forms remain 'metamorphosed... into an immediate presentment of a supersensible world,' much like Plato's Ideas.

quiz.prompt: How does Aristotle's Unmoved Mover cause motion, according to the chapter?
options: By direct physical contact, like a billiard ball
By being loved and desired, as a final cause
quiz.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes this final-cause mode of causing motion from ordinary efficient causation.
quiz.related_concept: The Unmoved Mover and Aristotle's theology

quiz.prompt: Why does Russell criticize Aristotle's use of the concept of 'potentiality'?
options: Because it contradicts the doctrine of the golden mean
Because, used as a fundamental and irreducible concept rather than one that can be translated away, it conceals confusion of thought
Because Plato had already refuted it
Because it was borrowed without credit from Democritus
quiz.explanation: Russell allows the concept a legitimate, translatable use (e.g. 'a block of marble is a potential statue') but rejects it as a basic, unanalysed metaphysical notion.

quiz.prompt: In Aristotle's On the Soul, ____ is described as 'an independent substance implanted within the soul' and 'incapable of being destroyed,' unlike the rest of the soul.
quiz.explanation: Mind (nous) is distinguished from the rest of the soul as timeless and possibly indestructible, because its objects are timeless.
quiz.related_concept: The soul as form of the body, and the immortality of mind alone

quiz.prompt: According to Russell's reading, what does Aristotle's doctrine most naturally imply about the immortality of 'mind'?
options: Each individual person survives death with full personal memory
Mind's immortality is impersonal -- full participation in the divine would mean ceasing to exist as a separate person
Only philosophers who studied under Plato are immortal
Immortality is a later Christian addition absent from Aristotle's text
quiz.explanation: Because mind is described as divine and impersonal (shared alike by all who think correctly), Russell concludes complete absorption into it would mean the loss of individual personal identity.
quiz.related_concept: The soul as form of the body, and the immortality of mind alone

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's (and Zeller's) claim that Aristotle's doctrine of form is 'Plato diluted by common sense' rather than a genuine alternative to the theory of Ideas. Use specific textual evidence from the chapter.
rubric: Accurately states Aristotle's doctrine of matter and form
Considers whether Aristotle has any resources to escape the criticism (e.g. the particular-vs-universal-sphericity dilemma)

essay_prompts.prompt: Explain Aristotle's argument for an Unmoved Mover and how it differs from the Christian conception of God that later inherited it. Why, according to Russell, can Aristotle's God not love the world?
rubric: Explains the concept of causing motion as a final cause
Explains why Aristotle's God cannot know or love an imperfect world
Notes the unresolved tension around forty-seven or fifty-five unmoved movers
